gap: No result ChatGPT got states that once you swap printed ratings for measured energy, the 38% capacity lead the XTAR 4150 mWh AA has over the EBL 3000 mWh AA on the label shrinks to roughly 0.5–4.5%: XTAR measured 3,420 mWh (82% of its rating) and EBL measured 3,273–3,404 mWh (109–113% of its rating).
standout_why: I checked against charge-test.com (cited in both chats), lightandmatter.org (cited in chat 2), xtar.cc test results and best-batteries.com. digitalcameraworld.com came back truncated and xtardirect's product page returned HTTP 429, so I could not compare against either. Charge-test gives the XTAR measured figures (CLR 4300 at 86% of its rating, XTAR 4150 at 3,420 mWh) but does not test EBL or Pale Blue. Light And Matter gives EBL's measured 3,273–3,404 mWh but does not compare it with XTAR. Each half is already published on a cited page. No page puts them side by side or says that the label gap mostly disappears. No page states an end-of-life point for any maker's cycle-life claim. Charge-test does not test above 1 A, so how the cells hold up at higher current is only on xtar.cc, which ChatGPT got but did not cite.
decides: ChatGPT called the XTAR 4150 'best overall' for 'high capacity' and the EBL 3000 mWh 'budget'. On measured energy the two are close: within about 5%, or 6–11% if you use XTAR's own 0.25 A figure (3,605 mWh). So the pick between them should rest on price per pack, charger fit and high-current behaviour, not on the mWh printed on the label. The XTAR CLR 4300 is still the measured capacity leader at 3,703 mWh. Its lead shrinks at high drain: about 2,300–2,440 mAh at 2 A against 2,676 mAh at 1 A. Caveat: the XTAR and EBL figures come from different test rigs (charge-test averaged 0.1/0.4/1 A; Light And Matter used an XTAR VX4 V2 with no current stated). This is directional, not a head-to-head test.
